newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine says U.S. aid "inadequate" for 1998.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine says U.S. aid "inadequate" for 1998.

text.p: Ukraine said on Friday it understood the need to boost economic reforms and uproot corruption to qualify for U.S aid in 1998 but complained the sum earmarked by the U.S. Senate was "inadequate".

The Senate, in its foreign aid package for the 1998 fiscal year, allocated $225 million to Ukraine but said half of the sum would only be released if the White House confirmed progress in the ex-Soviet state in reforms and an anti-corruption drive.

"Unfortunately there are some problems. And we should think here in terms of corruption and investment (climate) why such a resolution was adopted," Volodymyr Horbulin, Secretary of the policy-making Security and Defence Council, told reporters.
"But I think such aid is inadequate to what is happening here in Ukraine," he said adding Kiev should work to cultivate a Ukrainian "lobby" in Washington.
Ukraine received $300 million in 1996 and the same amount in 1997, which made it the third largest recipient of U.S. aid.
Some U.S. congressmen have threatened to cut all aid to Kiev unless its government shows a real commitment to deal with graft.
The U.S. lawmakers urged President Leonid Kuchma to create positive conditions for foreign investors.

U.S. telecommunication giant Motorola pulled out of Ukraine's GSM market in May. Several other U.S. companies complained about bribe-taking by Ukrainian officials and often changing "rules" governing the market.
Since then Kuchma has set up a special body to investigate corruption and organised crime and sacked his Prime Minister, Pavlo Lazarenko, seen as being slow in reforming the economy.
Last week Kuchma presented a programme for speeding up economic reforms and set up a special body to oversee them.
"That's true that reforms have been slowed down. To get aid you should carry out reforms," Ivan Zayats, a prominent member of parliamentary foreign affairs committee, told Reuters.
"There is a need also to fight mafia and corruption. We shouldn't pretend there is no corruption here," he added.

Recently Kuchma strongly criticised the West for not giving enough funds to assist with the closure of the Chernobyl nuclear station by the year 2000 and blamed the International Monetary Fund for not allocating a $2.5-$3 billion loan to Kiev.
